name: DNS
intent: Translate human-friendly names such as shop.example.com into the IP addresses computers connect to, using a worldwide chain of caches that trades freshness for speed.
scenario: A customer types shop.example.com. Before a single byte of the website moves, their device must learn which IP address that name currently points to.
problem: Computers route by IP address, but people use names, and addresses change when servers move or traffic is redirected. A single central phone book would be slow, a single point of failure and impossible to keep consistent worldwide. DNS is a distributed, cached, hierarchical directory, which makes lookups fast but changes slow to spread.

howItWorks.title: The browser and the operating system check their caches first
howItWorks.text: Most lookups never leave the device. The browser keeps recent answers, then the operating system does, each for the time the record allows. A cache hit costs well under a millisecond.

howItWorks.title: A recursive resolver does the work
howItWorks.text: On a miss, the device asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the internet provider or a public service. It has a large shared cache, so a name that anyone nearby asked recently is answered in tens of milliseconds.

howItWorks.title: On a cold miss the resolver walks the hierarchy
howItWorks.text: It asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks a .com server which servers handle example.com, and finally asks example.com's authoritative name server, which holds the real record. Each step is a network round trip, and the answer is cached at every level.

howItWorks.title: Every record carries a time to live (TTL)
howItWorks.text: The authoritative server says how long an answer may be cached, for example 300 seconds. Caches keep it until then and ask again afterwards. A long TTL means fewer lookups and faster pages; a short TTL means changes take effect sooner.

howItWorks.title: Use DNS deliberately for traffic management
howItWorks.text: DNS can return several addresses (round robin), different addresses depending on where the asker is (geo-routing to the nearest region), or an address that is only returned while the server is healthy. Lower the TTL before a planned move, and remember that some caches ignore short TTLs.

pros: Names stay stable while addresses change
Caching makes almost all lookups fast and keeps load off authoritative servers
The hierarchy scales to billions of names with no central bottleneck
Can steer users to the nearest or healthiest region
cons: Changes are not instant: old answers live in caches until the TTL expires
A cold lookup adds several round trips to the first request
DNS outages make a healthy service unreachable, and it is a target for attacks
Plain DNS is unencrypted unless DNS over HTTPS or TLS is used
whenToUse: Always: every public service needs a name
Geo-routing and failover between regions with a modest TTL
Separate names per service so each can move independently
whenNotToUse: As the only mechanism for fast failover: caches hold old answers, so combine it with load balancers and health checks
Very short TTLs everywhere, which turn your DNS provider into a bottleneck and cost every user extra lookups
pitfalls: Changing a record without lowering its TTL first, then waiting days for the world to catch up
A single DNS provider with no redundancy
Forgetting that clients and some resolvers cache longer than the TTL
Assuming that a DNS change is complete because it works from your laptop
